explanation: WHAT — the Class-I Euclidean gcd under its cascade name. ``gcd(a, 0) == a``, ``gcd(0, 0) == 0``, negatives and values past uint64 raise ValueError. Native dispatch goes through the cascade-namespace wrapper ``srmech_cascade_cyclic_gcd_u64``, itself a pure-delegation alias for the Class-I C primitive ``srmech_gcd``. WHEN — reach for it inside a cascade instead of ``math.gcd``: the value is identical, but this name is DSL-declarable, tool-schema discoverable and emitted by the introspect writer, whereas the stdlib call is invisible to all three. Use it for period commensurability (gear trains, dial realignment, ratio reduction) — the answer 1 is the useful one as often as the answer 235. SIBLING — READ THIS BEFORE YOU FILE A GAP: this is NOT a second implementation. ``srmech.math.cyclic.gcd`` (``srmech/math/cyclic.py:114``) is the SAME function; the cascade wrapper delegates to it and the worked run asserts the equality. The five modular peers ``cascade.cyclic_mod_add`` / ``_mod_mul`` / ``_mod_mul_wide`` / ``_mod_pow`` / ``_mod_inv`` (``srmech/cascade/compose.py:338`` / ``:316`` / ``:399`` / ``:358`` / ``:379``) stand in exactly the same relation to ``srmech.math.cyclic.mod_add`` / ``mod_mul`` / ``mod_mul_wide`` / ``mod_pow`` / ``mod_inv``. Note the one asymmetry: there is NO ``cascade.cyclic_lcm`` — reach for ``srmech.math.cyclic.lcm`` (``cyclic.py:162``) directly rather than composing gcd and a divide.
summary: Class I cyclic gcd (delegates to srmech.math.cyclic.gcd). The cascade-named alias for reaching the Class I primitive instead of math.gcd. Events emitted only when wrapped in `srmech.introspect.publish()` or `SRMECH_PUBLISH_STATUS=1` env-var set; otherwise silent.

explanation: WHAT - the Class-I Euclidean greatest common divisor of two NON-NEGATIVE integers, both bounded by uint64. Conventional edges: gcd(a, 0) == a and gcd(0, 0) == 0. A negative argument or one past 2**64 raises ValueError rather than silently wrapping; the C peer is srmech_gcd (c/include/srmech.h:1070), dispatched transparently when the native lib is loaded. WHEN - reach for it any time two periods, tooth counts or moduli must be reduced to their common sub-period: gear-train ratio reduction, dial realignment, reducing a (num, den) pair before it enters a Class-N chain. The answer 1 is as informative as the answer 235 - it is the proof that two cycles share no sub-period and therefore only realign at their lcm. SIBLINGS - READ THIS BEFORE FILING A GAP. srmech.cascade.cyclic_gcd (srmech/cascade/compose.py:263) is NOT a second implementation: it delegates straight here and the worked run asserts the equality, so do not re-derive one against the other. lcm (cyclic.py:162) is the dual question and is computed FROM this op, so never hand-roll a // gcd * b. primes.factor (primes.py:84) answers the finer question of WHICH primes are shared; this op answers only how much. rational.best_rational and rational_add call this as their reduction step, so a reduced (p, q) never needs a manual gcd afterwards. Do not reach for math.gcd inside a cascade: the value is identical, but the stdlib call is invisible to the DSL declarer, the tool schema and the introspect writer.
summary: Greatest common divisor of two non-negative integers.

explanation: WHAT - the least common multiple of two NON-NEGATIVE uint64 integers, computed as a // gcd(a, b) * b so the intermediate never overflows the way a * b // gcd would. lcm(a, 0) == 0 by the absorbing-zero convention (a deliberate value, not an error), and lcm(a, b) * gcd(a, b) == a * b for every non-zero pair - the identity the worked run checks. C peer srmech_lcm (c/include/srmech.h:1075). WHEN - the moment you need the RECURRENCE period of two cycles running together: when two dial pointers realign, when two gear trains repeat a configuration, the common denominator of two rational periods, the modulus a pair of congruences must share. WHEN NOT - if you only want to know WHETHER they share structure, gcd is the cheaper and more informative answer. SIBLINGS - gcd (cyclic.py:114) is this op's own first step and the dual reading of the same Euclidean run; never compute a * b // gcd(a, b) by hand, since the order of operations here is what keeps it in range. NOTE THE ASYMMETRY that trips readers: there IS a cascade-namespace cyclic_gcd (srmech/cascade/compose.py:263) but there is deliberately NO cascade.cyclic_lcm - call this op directly from a cascade rather than composing cyclic_gcd with a divide. primes.factor (primes.py:84) gives the prime-exponent maxima that this lcm is the product of, if you need to see WHY the answer is what it is.
summary: Least common multiple of two non-negative integers; 0 when either input is 0.

explanation: WHAT - the complete prime factorisation of n by trial division, returned as ASCENDING (prime, exponent) pairs whose product is exactly n. n < 2 returns the empty list, which keeps the product convention intact (an empty product is 1). Deterministic and exact; C peer srmech_factor (c/include/srmech.h:2635). WHEN - whenever the QUESTION is which primes, not how many: reading whether one period contains another, computing a totient or a divisor count, choosing a CRT split, deciding whether a modulus is squarefree, or explaining a gcd or lcm answer that surprised you. It also SUBSUMES the primality test - n is prime iff the result is a single pair with exponent 1 - so if you find yourself about to call is_prime and then factor, just call factor. COST: trial division is O(sqrt(n)), so a semiprime with two 32-bit factors is genuinely slow. There is no Pollard rho and no ECM here; that is a real bound. SIBLINGS - is_prime (primes.py:56) is the cheap membership answer when you do not need the decomposition. cyclic.gcd (srmech/math/cyclic.py:114) and cyclic.lcm (:162) answer the shared-structure question far more cheaply and should be preferred when the factor lists are only a means to that end - do not factor two numbers to compute their gcd. qprime.Qprime (srmech/amsc/qprime.py) is the CARRIER built on this output, holding a number as its prime-exponent vector so that multiply becomes add, gcd becomes min and lcm becomes max - reach for it rather than re-deriving exponent arithmetic over these pairs.
summary: Prime factorisation by trial division. Returns ascending (prime, exponent) pairs. n < 2 returns empty list.
